transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-06-15T10:00 PT
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Ava Thompson (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Sophie Patel (Rivermark Head of ML), Daniel Ruiz (Platform Eng), Maya Singh (SRE)
Links shared: perf spreadsheet (short link: bit.ly/rw-perf), draft kernel notes (gdoc link), initial benchmark logs (s3://rivermark-poc/logs)

Summary (auto): quick sync, some noise on live TTFT numbers due to warm vs cold starts, agreed to standardize benchmark harness and sequence-length buckets.

Transcript:
00:00 - Ava (Redwood): ok hey everyone thanks for joining, quick check-in on the latency tuning POC. we pushed the new kernel selections last night, Liam will walk through the TTFT and streaming numbers.
00:23 - Liam (Redwood SE): yeah, hi all. so immediate headline: TTFT improved on short sequences, for 128 tokens we see ~60-80ms TTFT cold, warm steady at ~35-45ms using the flash-attn path with the new triton kernels, um there is some variance on our side with the multi-gpu sharding.
00:48 - Sophie (Rivermark): when you say cold, you mean cold cache / cold KV? can you define the scenario.
00:55 - Liam: yeah sorry cold meaning empty KV cache and model uncached, so first request after a while. warm means KV warmed and model weights resident. that explains some 200-300ms outliers.
01:12 - Daniel (Customer): we're mainly concerned about the p99 for our interactive app, ideally <200ms p99 and TTFT as low as possible, we have some burst traffic up to 2k concurrent connections.
01:30 - Ava: right, and our goal this week was to focus on TTFT and streaming latency. we also tested streaming vs full-batch generate: streaming gives better perceived latency but can increase overall compute due to multiple kernel launches.
01:52 - Speaker 1 (transcript artifact): mm hmm, also there was that quantized int8 path that looked promising?
01:58 - Liam: yes, the int8 quantization helps throughput and reduces memory footprint, but the int8 kernels for mixed attention shapes are still maturing so we saw a couple of correctness diff tests failing on long sequences. we flagged that with the kernel team.
02:20 - Maya (SRE): do you have numbers for 512 and 1024 sequence lengths? most of our calls average 400-800 tokens after context.
02:30 - Liam: for 512 seq, TTFT cold is ~150-220ms, warm down to ~80-120ms with the flash-attn+kv cache path; for 1024 it's more like 300-420ms cold, warm ~130-220ms. again this depends on kernel selection — the baseline cuBLAS matmul + naive attention is slower.
02:52 - Sophie: how much of this is from GPU kernel choice vs network serialization / chunking?
03:00 - Liam: good question. we instrumented the path: kernel compute is ~60-75% of TTFT on long sequences, but there is nontrivial overhead from our streaming chunk assembly and python RPC in the harness. we think switching to the compiled client and optimizing chunk size gets another 10-20% wins.
03:25 - Daniel: any concerns with our VPC setup / vault / kms adding overhead?
03:32 - Ava: negligible for token-level latency, auth happens at session start; the crypto ops are async but we'll validate.
03:40 - Liam: note though when we do per-request key unwraps in HSM in the hot path, that will add tens of ms. recommend caching keys at session layer for the pilot.
03:55 - Maya: we can't cache keys for more than X minutes due to compliance, but we can negotiate a session TTL. we'll send policy.
04:05 - Speaker 2 (generic): there's also the prefix caching we tried — that helped a lot for repeated prompts.
04:12 - Liam: correct, prefix/KV caching reduces repeated compute; for our benchmark with 70% repeated prefixes we saw effective p50 drop by ~35%, p99 by ~20%. but for Rivermark's more varied prompts it's less effective, so we need the traffic profile.
04:35 - Sophie: ok we'll send the histograms.
04:40 - Ava: on kernel selection, we tried two configs: flash-attn + triton custom kernels, and an optimized cudnn/cuBLAS fallback. flash-attn wins for short to medium sequences, but on very long sequences the stitching kernels in our cuBLAS path are more stable.
05:05 - Liam: also important: batching policy. if you set batching window to 20ms you get better throughput but TTFT suffers for strict interactivity. we recommended dynamic batching with a latency SLO target to trade off.
05:25 - Daniel: what about streaming chunk size? any recommended defaults?
05:30 - Liam: we saw 8-16 token chunks hit a good tradeoff; 1-2 tokens increases kernel invocation overhead, 32 tokens increases perceived latency for first tokens. so start at 8 and tune.
05:45 - Sophie: you mentioned multi-gpu sharding issues earlier, can you expand?
05:50 - Liam: yeah on 2xA100 setup the KV cache cross-GPU sync added ~10-25ms depending on PCIe/NVLink topology; using partitioned KV with local prefetch reduces sync overhead but requires careful placement. we have notes in the gdoc.
06:12 - Ava: can we run a dedicated benchmark that mirrors your production concurrency (2k concurrent) but with our standard sequence buckets? that'll help validate p99.
06:20 - Daniel: yes we can spin up a harness to replay traffic but need the exact script.
06:25 - Liam: we'll provide a harness example and the expected request distribution. we'll also include options for warm vs cold runs.
06:40 - Speaker 1: small nit, the logs show some transcription of model names as "Ruddwood" in our artifact, ignore that.
06:48 - Ava: haha noted.
06:50 - Liam: on quantization again — int8 path with the current kernels gives throughput wins but the word error rate on some prompts nudges up slightly. for safety-critical responses you probably want int8 with post-quant evals or stick to fp16 for now.
07:10 - Sophie: acceptable; we'll run targeted QA on our critical prompt set.
07:18 - Daniel: anything on model variants? could fallback to a smaller model for high concurrency bursts?
07:23 - Ava: yes policy-based routing is supported; can route by latency/cost. fallback to a quantized smaller model reduces cost and preserves availability. we can demo that.
07:34 - Maya: we need to log every decision for audit, can Redwood emit audit logs and token-level cost traces?
07:40 - Liam: yes, console exposes per-request timelines, kernel selection metadata, and audit logs; we'll include an example log format.
07:50 - Sophie: security/compliance piece — can you confirm SOC 2 and ISO status? we need SOC two type 2 reports.
07:58 - Ava: Redwood has SOC 2 type II in our compliance pack; we'll share the redacted report and our data retention policy.
08:08 - Daniel: awesome.
08:12 - Liam: ok next, on the benchmark plan: we'll run three buckets 128/512/1024, both cold and warm. for each we will measure TTFT, p50/p95/p99, and token throughput. we will run with streaming chunk sizes 8 and 16, and with int8 and fp16 kernels.
08:35 - Sophie: can you also include an experiment with batching window 0/10/20ms?
08:38 - Liam: yes.
08:40 - Ava: timeline wise, Liam to run the benchmarks by Fri (2027-06-18), we share results early next week and sync the following Tue.
08:50 - Maya: I'll send the traffic histograms today.
08:54 - Daniel: and I'll circulate the target SLO doc.
09:00 - Speaker 2: small point on tooling: try to use the compiled client instead of python harness to reduce RPC overhead.
09:06 - Liam: agreed, compiled client reduces per-request serialization by ~8-12ms in our tests.
09:14 - Sophie: anything we should change in our infra? Maya?
09:18 - Maya: we'll allocate a test VPC with similar network topology and make sure nvlink topology is representative.
09:25 - Ava: perfect.
09:28 - Liam: also will include kernel perf traces (nvprof/pt) for the hot paths and a short explanation of where time is spent.
09:35 - Sophie: that helps, thanks.
09:40 - Ava: ok to recap real quick — action items: Ava share perf sheet and kernel notes, Liam run multi-seq benchmarks (128/512/1024, streaming chunk 8/16, int8/fp16, batching windows 0/10/20ms) and send results by 6/18, Rivermark to send traffic histograms and SLOs by 6/17, schedule follow-up week of 6/21.
10:05 - Daniel: sounds good.
10:10 - Sophie: thanks everyone.
10:15 - Meeting end.

Notes on transcription artifacts: some speaker labels show Speaker 1/2; proper nouns like "Redwood" sometimes transcribed as "Ruddwood"; technical acronyms occasionally spelled out (SOC two). These are present in raw Fireflies export.
